Causes of the Great War

Imperial Rivalry, the Arms Race & The Thirty Days of Madness (1871–1914)
Overarching Historical Enquiry
“How did decades of imperial rivalry and fear culminate in thirty days of madness?”
Primary Visual Plate: Royal Navy battleship HMS Dreadnought at sea (c. 1906–1907) Imperial War Museum Photographic Archive
Curriculum Synopsis • The Powder Keg of Europe

For forty years following the 1871 unification of Germany, the European Great Powers preserved an uneasy armed peace through intricate alliances, imperial expansion, and massive dreadnought construction. In this master enquiry workbook, pupils investigate how long-term militarism, colonial jealousy in Africa, and rigid railway mobilisations transformed two pistol shots in Sarajevo into the unprecedented catastrophe of the First World War.

The 6 Disciplinary Enquiries:
L1: Creation of the German Empire (1871)
L4: Dreadnought & The Naval Arms Race
L2: Franco-Prussian War & Alsace-Lorraine
L5: The Alliance System: Peace or Trap?
L3: The Scramble for Africa & Weltpolitik
L6: Sarajevo & The Thirty-Seven Days of Crisis
Living Unit Timeline • Part I: The Road to Armed Peace (1871–1904)

The European Balance of Power

Pages 2–3 Facing Spread
Living Timeline Protocol: Throughout this unit, sketch each historical milestone inside its dedicated frame. Add dates, flags, and causal arrows. Spine • Facing Left
⌜Milestone Sketchpad⌝
[Sketch: Hall of Mirrors / Pickelhaube helmet]
⌞1871 Unification⌟
1871 Proclamation of the German Empire at Versailles

Following the crushing defeat of Napoleon III at Sedan, King Wilhelm I of Prussia is proclaimed Kaiser in the French Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. Germany annexes Alsace-Lorraine and imposes a 5-billion franc fine, permanently alienating France and shattering the European balance of power.

Key Enquiry Link: Lessons 1 & 2 • Power shift to Berlin • French territorial loss • Bismarck's isolation policy
⌜Milestone Sketchpad⌝
[Sketch: Triple Alliance pact / 3 Eagle crests]
⌞1882 Alliance⌟
1882 Formation of the Triple Alliance

Bismarck forms a secret defensive military pact between Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy. Bismarck’s primary strategic objective is to keep France diplomatically isolated and deprived of continental allies, preventing any coalition from threatening Germany with a two-front war.

Key Enquiry Link: Lesson 5 • The alliance system as a defensive deterrent • Bismarck's diplomatic web
⌜Milestone Sketchpad⌝
[Sketch: Punch cartoon 'Dropping the Pilot']
⌞1890 Dismissal⌟
1890 Kaiser Wilhelm II Dismisses Bismarck: The Launch of Weltpolitik

The young, impetuous Kaiser Wilhelm II forces Bismarck to resign, abandons the secret Reinsurance Treaty with Russia, and embarks on Weltpolitik—demanding Germany's "Place in the Sun" through an aggressive global empire and a high-seas battle fleet. Russia immediately turns to France.

Key Enquiry Link: Lessons 3 & 4 • End of diplomatic caution • Franco-Russian alliance (1894) • Encirclement fear
⌜Milestone Sketchpad⌝
[Sketch: Battleship guns / Entente handshake]
⌞1904 Entente⌟
1898–04 German Naval Laws & The Anglo-French Entente Cordiale

Admiral Tirpitz passes the German Navy Laws to build a fleet capable of challenging Britain. Alarmed by German naval expansion and imperial bluster, Great Britain abandons "Splendid Isolation" in 1904, signing the historic Entente Cordiale with France and resolving all colonial disputes.

Key Enquiry Link: Lessons 3 & 5 • Two-Power Standard • Polarization of Europe into two armed camps
Living Timeline Synthesis Challenge • The Diplomatic Shift (1871–1904) Causal Linkage Check

Living Unit Timeline • Part II: Crises & The Spark (1905–1914)

The Escalation to Total War

Pages 2–3 Facing Spread
Living Timeline Protocol: Trace the countdown from the Dreadnought revolution to the Sarajevo assassination and Belgian invasion. Spine • Facing Right
1906 Launch of HMS Dreadnought: The Naval Revolution

The Royal Navy launches HMS Dreadnought in Portsmouth. Powered by revolutionary steam turbines and mounting ten 12-inch guns, it renders every pre-existing battleship obsolete overnight. Germany immediately widens the Kiel Canal and begins building Nassau-class dreadnoughts.

Key Enquiry Link: Lesson 4 • Naval arms race • Public hysteria ("We want eight and we won't wait!")
⌜Milestone Sketchpad⌝
[Sketch: Dreadnought 12-inch gun turret]
⌞1906 Dreadnought⌟
1908–11 Bosnian Crisis & The Agadir Incident

Austria-Hungary annexes Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1908, infuriating Serbia and humiliating Russia. In 1911, Germany sends the gunboat Panther to Morocco. Britain intervenes forcefully on France’s side, conducting secret joint military staff talks for European troop deployment.

Key Enquiry Link: Lessons 3 & 5 • The Balkan Powder Keg • Serbian nationalist underground • Panther gunboat
⌜Milestone Sketchpad⌝
[Sketch: SMS Panther gunboat / Balkan map]
⌞1911 Agadir⌟
28 June 1914 Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo

Nineteen-year-old Bosnian Serb nationalist Gavrilo Princip shoots Archduke Franz Ferdinand and Sophie at point-blank range on Franz Josef Street. Princip is armed and trained by the clandestine Serbian military network, The Black Hand. The fatal wrong turn ignites the July Crisis.

Key Enquiry Link: Lesson 6 • Fatal wrong turn • FN Browning semi-automatic pistol • Black Hand conspiracy
⌜Milestone Sketchpad⌝
[Sketch: Browning pistol / Stalled open car]
⌞Sarajevo Spark⌟
July–Aug 1914 The July Crisis & The Outbreak of Total War

Backed by Germany’s "Blank Cheque", Austria-Hungary issues an ultimatum and declares war on Serbia. Russia mobilizes; Germany declares war on Russia and France, invading neutral Belgium under the Schlieffen Plan. Great Britain declares war on Germany on 4 August to defend the 1839 Treaty of London.

Key Enquiry Link: Lesson 6 • The July Crisis Domino Sequence • Treaty of London (1839) • World War
⌜Milestone Sketchpad⌝
[Sketch: 4 August declaration / Belgian border]
⌞1914 World War⌟

Distinguish between Bismarck’s ruthless, pragmatic Realpolitik (practical power and national interest) and democratic Liberalism (speeches and majority votes):
Task 4: Archival Interrogation & Annotation: Bismarck’s "Blood and Iron" Speech (1862)
Source A: Otto von Bismarck Addresses the Prussian Budget Commission (30 Sept 1862) PRUSSIAN STATE ARCHIVES · PARLIAMENTARY PROCEEDINGS · BERLIN
“Prussia must concentrate and maintain its power for the favorable moment which has already been missed several times. Prussia’s borders according to the treaties of Vienna are not favorable to a healthy state life. Not through speeches and majority decisions will the great questions of the day be decided—that was the great mistake of 1848 and 1849—but by iron and blood (Eisen und Blut).”
Provenance: Speech by Minister-President Otto von Bismarck to the Budget Committee of the Prussian House of Representatives, Berlin, 1862.
✏️ Active Source Annotation Protocol:
① Underline: phrase proving Bismarck rejected parliamentary voting.
② Circle: the treaty borders Bismarck declared "unfavorable" to Prussia.
③ Box: the dual physical elements Bismarck believed decided history.
1. Historical Inference: What can a historian infer from Source A about why Bismarck rejected constitutional democracy in favor of autocratic military force?
2. Contextual Explanation: Explain how Bismarck’s statecraft between 1862 and 1871 proved that "iron and blood" was Prussian state policy rather than mere rhetoric:

Core Vocabulary & Conceptual Precision
Distinguish between Britain’s Two-Power Standard (Royal Navy equal to next two navies combined) and Admiral Tirpitz’s Risk Theory (German navy strong enough that attacking it would risk Britain’s supremacy):
Task 4: Archival Interrogation: Fisher’s Confidential Memo & Technical Dreadnought Comparison
Source C: First Sea Lord Admiral Sir John Fisher, Confidential Admiralty Memorandum (Dec 1906) BRITISH ADMIRALTY ARCHIVES · ADM 1/7892 · LONDON
“My principles are: Speed is armor. Hit first, hit hard, and keep on hitting... The Dreadnought has rendered all existing battleships obsolete. If Germany builds one, we must build two. The Empire floats upon the Royal Navy; if the navy is defeated, we are starved into surrender in three weeks.”
Design FeaturePre-Dreadnought (HMS King Edward VII, 1903)HMS Dreadnought (1906 Breakthrough)
Main Armament 4 × 12-inch heavy guns + mixed smaller calibres 10 × 12-inch guns (all-big-gun uniform battery)
Broadside Firepower 4 heavy shells per minute 8 heavy shells per minute (2.5× destructive energy)
Propulsion & Speed Triple-expansion reciprocating steam (18 knots) Parsons steam turbines (21 knots top speed)
Strategic Effect Dominant over older fleets; vulnerable to speed Made all 150 battleships in the world obsolete overnight

Low-Floor Clue: Notice the broadside firepower jumped from 4 to 8 heavy shells—any navy with dreadnoughts could destroy older ships from miles away. ★ Scholar’s Edge: How did the naval race transform the Entente Cordiale from a friendly colonial agreement into a binding, de facto military alliance?

Task 4: Archival Interrogation: The Desperate "Willy-Nicky" Telegrams (29–31 July 1914)
TELEGRAM 1: CZAR NICHOLAS II TO KAISER WILHELM II (29 July, 1:00 am)
“To try and avoid such a calamity as a European war, I beg you in the name of our old friendship to do what you can to stop your ally [Austria] from going too far. I foresee that very soon I shall be overwhelmed by the pressure brought upon me, and be forced to take extreme measures which will lead to war.”
RUSSIAN IMPERIAL FOREIGN ARCHIVE · ST PETERSBURG
TELEGRAM 2: KAISER WILHELM II TO CZAR NICHOLAS II (29 July, 6:30 pm)
“I cannot consider Austria’s action against Serbia as an ‘ignoble’ war... In this action, Austria is defending her very existence. If you mobilize against Austria, my role as mediator will be endangered if not ruined. The whole weight of the decision lies on your shoulders now, who have to bear the responsibility for Peace or War.”
GERMAN IMPERIAL ARCHIVE · AUSWÄRTIGES AMT · BERLIN
✏️ Active Telegraph Annotation Protocol:
① Underline: Nicholas II’s plea invoking their personal friendship.
② Circle: the phrase showing Nicholas was pressured by his military generals.
③ Box: Wilhelm’s warning that Russian mobilization would trigger war.
1. Diplomatic Analysis: What does the intimate, desperate tone of these telegrams reveal about the power of personal monarchical diplomacy versus the unstoppable momentum of military alliances in 1914?
2. Structural Inevitability: Explain why neither the Kaiser nor the Tsar was able to halt the countdown to war despite their mutual desire to avoid bloodshed:
Low-Floor Clue: Notice both cousins blame each other’s allies—the rigid alliance treaties meant once military mobilization started, emperors were prisoners of their generals. ★ Scholar’s Edge: How does the Willy-Nicky exchange support Christopher Clark’s thesis in "The Sleepwalkers" that European rulers were blind to the trap their alliances had created?

Causes of the Great War (1871–1914) • Master Review

Unit Revision Hub
The M-A-I-N Framework of Long-Term Causes:
[M] MILITARISM

The Anglo-German naval arms race (Dreadnoughts); rigid railway mobilization timetables (Schlieffen Plan); glorification of armed combat as national duty.

[A] ALLIANCES

The Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) vs. The Triple Entente (Britain, France, Russia). Intended as deterrence, but acted as a doomsday machine.

[I] IMPERIALISM

Kaiser Wilhelm II’s aggressive demand for a "Place in the Sun" (Weltpolitik); clashes over Morocco (Tangier 1905, Agadir 1911); partition of Africa.

[N] NATIONALISM

French desire for revanche over Alsace-Lorraine; Pan-Slavic nationalism in the Balkans; Serbian underground networks (The Black Hand).

Historiographical Debate: Who Was to Blame?
Fritz Fischer (1961): Argued that imperial Germany bore primary responsibility by deliberately provoking a European war via the "Blank Cheque" to break out of encirclement and achieve world power status.
Christopher Clark (2012): Argued in The Sleepwalkers that all European powers shared blame. Leaders were blind to the catastrophic risks of their diplomatic maneuvers, sleepwalking into a tragedy none truly wanted.
